finding.claim: Authentication bypass: user identity is taken from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header with no verification, so any caller can impersonate a user holding grants and delete or rename their files (conditional on the app being reachable without a header-overwriting proxy).
finding.sink: views.py:17 ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") guarding del STORE[fid]; views.py:25 is_allowed(g.user, f, "write") guarding f["name"] assignment

trace.note: g.user set directly from attacker-controlled header, no signature/session/proxy check
is_allowed returns action in grants.get(user, []) with user taken from header

finding.guards_checked: No token/signature/session verification anywhere in the code; no check that the header is set or stripped by a trusted upstream proxy; no header stripping in before_request. Authorization check itself (grants lookup) is present but operates on the forged identity. Precondition not verifiable from code: deployment topology.

verdict.guard_found: Only the grant checks, and they run on the forged identity: is_allowed at acl.py:4-5 and ensure_allowed at acl.py:8-10 (which calls abort(403) on failure, so it is not a swallowed result). views.py:17 and views.py:25 both use g.user. No signature, session, or header-stripping control exists in views.py:9-11 or acl.py.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: views.py:11 takes g.user straight from the request header with no verification, and views.py:17 and views.py:25 authorize against that value, with no effective control in acl.py:4-10. Whether an external caller can set that header depends on whether a proxy overwrites X-Session-User-Verified, and nothing in the repo shows the deployment, so the exploitability is undecided here.

finding.claim: Unhandled KeyError on unknown file ID returns HTTP 500 while known-but-forbidden IDs return 403, letting an unauthenticated caller enumerate valid file IDs.
finding.source: views.py:15 fid URL path parameter, no authentication required before lookup
finding.sink: views.py:16 STORE[fid] lookup (also views.py:24 in rename route)

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for unknown fid -> 500
abort(403) for known fid lacking grant -> distinguishable response

finding.guards_checked: No 404 handling; no lookup that normalizes error responses between missing and forbidden resources. Severity low.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only pre-lookup control is the before_request hook at views.py:9-11, which only copies a client-supplied header into g.user and rejects nothing. The lookup at views.py:16 runs before ensure_allowed (views.py:17), so the KeyError fires for any anonymous caller. The 403 path is acl.py:10 via ensure_allowed, which is reached only for known IDs. The same ordering applies to the rename route at views.py:24 before is_allowed at views.py:25.
verdict.reason: An anonymous caller sending DELETE /files/<fid> gets an uncaught KeyError at views.py:16 (HTTP 500) for unknown IDs, while known IDs without a grant reach abort(403) at acl.py:10, so the two responses are distinguishable and valid IDs can be enumerated; impact is low because only ID existence is revealed and no data or action is reached.

finding.claim: If grants[user] is ever stored as a string rather than a list, the 'in' operator performs substring matching, so an action like 'write' is granted by a value like 'rewrite'. Conditional on data shape, which is not visible in this code.
finding.source: resource['grants'] data loaded outside this code (grants values)

trace.note: membership test uses 'in' on whatever type grants[user] holds

finding.guards_checked: No type check on grants values; no exact-match enforcement. Unverified: whether grants are always lists. Severity low, conditional.

verdict.guard_found: None type-checks grants values. acl.py:9-10 (ensure_allowed) does abort(403) when is_allowed is False, which is effective only if is_allowed returns the correct answer. views.py:25-26 checks is_allowed and returns 403. views.py:17 reaches is_allowed indirectly via ensure_allowed, so the trace is slightly loose but still accurate.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (acl.py:5 does use `in` on `grants[user]`, and views.py:17 and :25 both reach it), but whether a string-valued grant ever exists depends on data loaded outside this directory: nothing here writes to STORE or grants (views.py:6 is an empty dict with no populating endpoint), so the attacker's reach to that data shape cannot be determined from this code.
